editorial.title: Star ratings get gamed. Source documents don't.
editorial.p1: TrustGive aggregates public registries — IRS Form 990, UK Charity Commission, Минюст СОНКО — and links directly to the source documents. We don't publish a trust score. We don't process payments. The job of the platform is to take you to the original record in one click.

notChecked.body: We confirmed that this organisation is registered with its regulator and has filed the accounts linked above. We did not assess how well it spends the money, how much of it reaches the work, or whether it is a good place for your donation. Nothing on this page is a recommendation — a verified badge means a document exists and opens, nothing more.

about.title: About
about.lead: TrustGive is built and run by one person. It takes no money from charities, runs no ads, and has no investors. Here is who I am and what that means for what you're reading.
about.whoBody: I'm Alex Diachenko. I build software, and I live in Moscow. TrustGive started as a weekend question and turned into the thing I work on. There is no team behind it — when this site is wrong, it's my mistake, and when it's fixed, I fixed it.
about.whyBody1: I went to donate and stopped at a question I couldn't answer: who decides which charities are real? The large rating sites publish scores whose method I couldn't follow, and which nonprofits learn to work around — Charity Navigator dropped its overhead-ratio metric in 2023 for that reason. The donation platforms add 10–18% on top of a gift before the charity sees it.
about.whyBody2: So this site doesn't score anything. It finds the filing the regulator holds and links straight to it. You read the document and decide. Donations happen on the charity's own site, not here.
about.moneyBody: It isn't. Infrastructure costs about nothing — a small database, a worker, free public APIs. Charities cannot pay to be listed, to rank higher, or to be removed. There is no revenue to protect, which is the only reason I can afford to delist an organisation the moment its filing stops resolving.
about.limitsBody: Three limits worth knowing before you rely on anything here:
about.limit1: A verified badge means the organisation is registered and has filed. It says nothing about whether the money is spent well. That's a harder question and I don't answer it.
about.limit2: Coverage follows the registers, not the sector. Countries whose regulators publish machine-readable records are represented; countries whose regulators don't are missing, regardless of how good their charities are.
about.limit3: Filings run one to two years behind. That's the regulator's cycle, not a gap in the data.
about.errorBody: Tell me. I've already found four organisations listed under another entity's registration number — one of them filed under the Gates Foundation. I found those by auditing my own data, but I won't catch everything. A specific report with the charity's name gets fixed faster than a general complaint.
about.openBody: The code, the method and the API are public. You don't have to take my word for how verification works — you can read the code that does it, or query the same data directly.

research.title: Research
research.lead: Findings from auditing this catalogue. Published because they hold outside it: anyone assembling charity data from public registers runs into the same walls, and most of them are invisible until you hit one.
research.footnote: Every figure published here is reproducible from the script and the public API linked in each piece. If you find a number that doesn't hold up, hello@trustgive.org.
research.linkScript: The script that produces these figures
research.linkSources: Which registers the data comes from
research.unknownBody: This research piece doesn't exist. It may have been renamed — the index lists everything published.

how-old-is-charity-financial-data.title: Nobody can tell you what a charity spent last year
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.standfirst: Across 365 organisations whose filings we could open, not one has financial information covering a period that ended within the last twelve months. Not one. The median is two and a half years old, and that is the system working as designed.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s1p1: For each of {{measured}} published organisations we took the most recent filing anyone can currently obtain, and asked how long ago the fiscal period it describes came to an end.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s1p2: That is a narrower question than “how slow is the regulator”, and deliberately so. We don't store the date a return was received or published, so we can't speak to regulator speed. What we can measure is what a reader gets when they go looking today — which is the question a donor actually has.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2Title: The freshest thing available is two and a half years old
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2p1: The median filing describes a period that ended {{median}} months ago. {{older}} of {{measured}} — 94% — describe a period more than two years gone. The top row of the table is the one worth sitting with.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s2p2: Zero. Not a small number: none. Whatever a donor is told about how a charity spends money, nobody — not this site, not any rating service, not the regulator's own website — can currently show them a filing about the year that just ended.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3Title: It is a sawtooth, not a delay
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3p1: The filing dates cluster hard, because fiscal years end on a handful of dates and everything downstream follows:
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s3p2: A charity closes its books on 31 December, has months to file, the regulator processes and publishes, and a mirror picks it up. Each step is reasonable; stacked, they put two and a half years between the money being spent and anyone outside being able to read about it. The lag isn't negligence, and it isn't going to be fixed by anyone shouting at a charity.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4Title: Countries differ, but far less than you'd expect
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4p1: Median age of the freshest available filing, by country:
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s4p2: Six months separates the fastest from the slowest — nothing like the coverage gaps in the companion piece, where the same countries range from 100% to zero. The spread within a country tells you more: UK filings sit in a tight band of {{gbMin}} to {{gbMax}} months, because one regulator publishes on one cycle, while the US stretches to {{usMax}} months at the far end, where an organisation's most recent machine-readable return is years behind.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s5p1: “Verified” and “current” are different claims, and only the first one is available. A revenue figure on this site — or on any site built from public filings — describes a year that ended long before you read it. That is worth knowing before treating it as a picture of a charity today.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.s5p2: It also sets a ceiling on what charity data can do. Any question of the form “is this organisation in trouble right now” cannot be answered from filings, by anyone, and a service that implies otherwise is selling the appearance of currency rather than the thing.
how-old-is-charity-financial-data.method: Measured {{date}} across the {{measured}} published organisations carrying a filing date; 4 more carry none. The figure is the age of the fiscal period the filing covers (ProPublica's `tax_prd`, or the equivalent period end for other registers), not the date the return was submitted or published. Buckets are exclusive; percentages are of the 365 measured.

what-we-could-not-verify.title: A third of the charities we assembled could not be verified — and it was almost never their fault
what-we-could-not-verify.standfirst: 541 organisations went in. 369 came out with a regulator document you can open. The 172 that didn't cluster by country, not by charity, and the reason is what the regulator publishes — not what the organisation does.
what-we-could-not-verify.s1p1: We assembled {{assembled}} organisations from public registers and tried to link each one to a document its own regulator published — a filing, a register entry, something a reader can open and check. {{verified}} of them made it.
what-we-could-not-verify.s1p2: The other {{unverified}} are not published. They stay in the database, and they reappear the moment a document can be found for them, but a directory whose claim is “every entry links to the regulator's own file” cannot carry entries that don't.
what-we-could-not-verify.s2Title: The failure is not broken links
what-we-could-not-verify.s2p1: This is the part that surprised us. Of the {{unverified}} unverified organisations, {{noDocument}} had no obtainable document at all — not a dead link, an absent one. Exactly {{deadLink}} had a document whose link stopped resolving.
what-we-could-not-verify.s2p2: So the common mental model — records rot, links die, catalogues decay — describes almost none of this. The records were never obtainable in the first place. That distinction matters, because the two problems have different fixes: rot needs monitoring, absence needs a different source.
what-we-could-not-verify.s3p1: Sorting the same 541 records by country makes the pattern obvious. The verification rate has almost nothing to do with the organisations and almost everything to do with whether their regulator publishes a stable, per-organisation record that a machine can fetch and a human can read.
what-we-could-not-verify.s3p2: The United Kingdom is at 100% because the Charity Commission gives every registered charity a permanent page keyed to its registration number. The United States is at 87% because the IRS releases Form 990 data that ProPublica mirrors with a stable URL per organisation. At the other end sit countries whose registers exist but are search-only: you can look an organisation up by hand, but there is no address to link to, so there is nothing to show a reader.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4Title: Canada, and a check that would have lied
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p1: Canada is the sharpest case: {{tested}} organisations assembled, none published. It is also where we caught our own worst near-miss.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p2: The first verification routine written for Canada accepted a registration number if the CRA's charity page returned HTTP 200. Tested against controls, that page returns 200 for a fabricated number — byte-for-byte the same 55,230-byte response as for a real one. Had that routine run, it would have stamped “verified” on every Canadian record including the invented controls. It was disabled before it ever ran.
what-we-could-not-verify.s4p3: Checking the same numbers against a CRA endpoint that returns data rather than a status code gave a different answer: {{genuine}} of {{tested}} resolved to the right organisation, {{wrongEntity}} resolved to a different organisation entirely — one of them to a local parish rather than the national body whose name we had stored — and {{unresolvable}} did not resolve at all. A government-issued identifier that renders on a page is not evidence that it belongs to the organisation next to it.
what-we-could-not-verify.s5Title: What this means if you use charity data
what-we-could-not-verify.s5p1: Two things worth carrying away. First, coverage of any charity directory reflects regulator publishing practice, not sector quality — so an organisation's absence from a directory says far less than its presence. Second, if you are building verification of your own, never accept an HTTP status as proof; require a response that names the organisation, and compare that name to the one you hold.
what-we-could-not-verify.s5p2: We publish only what survives that test, which is why this catalogue is smaller than the data we hold. The gap is the finding.
what-we-could-not-verify.method: Figures measured {{date}} across all records in the database, published and unpublished. “Verified” means at least one source document whose URL returned HTTP 200 at audit time and whose registry record names the organisation. The Canadian identifier testing, including the fabricated controls, is recorded in the project's data-integrity audit.

api.title: Public API
api.lead: The whole catalogue is available as JSON. No key, no account, nothing to sign up for — the endpoints this site runs on are the ones you can query.
api.accessBody: Read-only and anonymous. Responses carry cache headers and are served from the edge, so repeated requests are cheap for both of us.
api.rateLimitValue: 60 requests per minute per IP address
api.endpointsBody: Every endpoint below is a GET and needs no headers.

endpoint.list: Paginated catalogue with filters — the main entry point.
endpoint.detail: One organisation in full: financials, source documents, press mentions.
endpoint.documents: Just the source documents held for one organisation.
endpoint.featured: The homepage selection, plus the real catalogue total.
endpoint.hubs: Country, cause and registry sections with their counts.
endpoint.stats: Catalogue size, countries covered, and when it was last re-checked.
endpoint.causes: The cause taxonomy, in English and Russian.
endpoint.seo: The question-and-verdict payload behind the “Is X a legitimate charity?” pages.

api.exampleBody: Look an organisation up by name or registration number:
api.termsBody: The catalogue is assembled from public registers, and every record links to the document its regulator published. TrustGive claims no licence over those documents: if you intend to redistribute the filings themselves, the terms are the register's, and each register states its own.
api.termsLink: Which registers the data comes from
api.schemaBody: The OpenAPI 3.1 schema is generated from the code on every deploy, so it can't drift from what the API actually does. Point a client generator at it, or read it in the browser.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.lead: Everything in the catalogue comes from a public register. This page lists which ones, what each covers, and where each falls short.
sources.howBody: A nightly job re-reads every US filing from ProPublica and re-checks every source link in the catalogue. A charity whose link stops resolving is removed from public view the same night — not flagged, removed. Nothing here is entered by hand except the two-sentence descriptions and the translations.

propublica.name: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
propublica.meta: United States · Form 990 · free, no key
propublica.body: Mirrors the IRS release of Form 990 filings for US 501(c)(3) organisations. Supplies the registration number, the fiscal period covered, total revenue and executive compensation. This is the largest single source in the catalogue.
propublica.limit: Filings appear one to two years after the fiscal year ends, and the API returns nothing for organisations that file on paper or fall below the electronic filing threshold.

charityCommission.name: Charity Commission for England and Wales
charityCommission.body: The statutory register of charities in England and Wales, with accounts and annual returns filed against each registration number.
charityCommission.limit: Covers England and Wales only. Scottish and Northern Irish charities sit under separate regulators that are not yet integrated here.

acnc.name: Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
acnc.body: The national charity register, matched to the Australian Business Register record for each organisation.
acnc.limit: The register does not expose per-charity revenue, so Australian entries carry a verified registration without a money breakdown. Several national bodies share a domain with their state branches, which makes automatic matching unreliable — those are resolved by hand or left out.

minjust.name: Минюст СОНКО
minjust.body: The Ministry of Justice register of socially oriented non-profit organisations, used for the small curated Russian selection.
minjust.limit: Registration confirms legal existence and nothing else. Russian entries are curated rather than loaded in bulk, and the legal exclusions described in the methodology apply.

sources.missingBody: Coverage follows what regulators publish, not what matters. Two absences are worth naming:
sources.missingCanada: Canada. The CRA charity register has no stable public address for an individual charity — the URL that looks like one returns an identical page for every input, including invented registration numbers, and an error in a browser. There is no document to link to, so no Canadian charity is published here.
sources.missingEurope: Most of continental Europe. Charity registers are national and heterogeneous; many publish no machine-readable per-organisation record, and smaller organisations file only on paper.
sources.useBody: The same records the site reads are available from the public API, unauthenticated. If you are citing the catalogue in research, query it directly rather than scraping the pages — and note the date, because entries are removed when their evidence stops resolving.

methodology.title: How we verify
methodology.lead: We don't grade charities. We show you the documents that grade them for us — and link straight to those documents.
methodology.verifiedMeansBody: A charity is marked Verified on TrustGive if all three are true: (1) it is registered with at least one government registry; (2) it has filed financial documents in the last 24 months; (3) we link directly to those documents on the charity's page.
methodology.catalogueTitle: Why this catalogue is smaller than it could be
methodology.catalogueBody: Every organisation listed here has a regulator filing you can open in one click. If we cannot confirm that document, the organisation does not appear at all — we don't publish it with a caveat, a lower rating, or an "unverified" label. A directory that mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries quietly transfers the checking work back to you, which defeats the purpose.
methodology.catalogueBody2: This has a cost we'd rather state than hide: real, reputable charities are missing from these pages. Some national registers publish no per-organisation record we can link to, and some organisations file only on paper. Their absence is a limitation of what we can prove, not a judgement about them. If a charity you trust isn't here, that is the most likely reason.
methodology.doNotVerifyBody: We do not assess program effectiveness, mission outcomes, or donor satisfaction. For deeper rigor, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.
methodology.complianceBody: TrustGive is operated from Russia. Russian law requires us to exclude the following categories of organisations from our catalogue, regardless of the work they do:
methodology.complianceItem1: Organisations recognised as foreign agents by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation
methodology.complianceItem2: Organisations recognised as extremist or undesirable by Russian courts or executive bodies
methodology.complianceItem3: Organisations providing material assistance to parties of active armed conflicts
methodology.complianceItem4: Organisations registered in territories where compliance with Russian regulations cannot be reliably verified
methodology.complianceFooter: These exclusions are a legal compliance requirement, not an editorial judgement about the work these organisations do. Donors who wish to support such organisations can do so directly through other discovery tools.
methodology.deeperBody: For mission-effectiveness analysis, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.
